arml-1998-power-01a.title: Bounds and attainment
arml-1998-power-01a.body:
From $A\le B\le C$ and $A+B+C=180$: $3A\le180$, so $A\le60$; $2B\le B+C=180-A\le179$, so $B\le89$; $3C\ge180$, so $C\ge60$; and $C=180-A-B\le178$ since $A,B\ge1$.

Every value in these ranges occurs: $(A,B,C)=(A,A,180-2A)$ for $A=1,\dots,60$; $(1,B,179-B)$ for $B=1,\dots,89$ (valid because $B\le179-B$); and for $C$: $(1,179-C,C)$ when $C\ge90$, and for $60\le C\le 89$ take $(\frac{180-C}2,\frac{180-C}2,C)$ if $C$ is even and $(\frac{179-C}2,\frac{181-C}2,C)$ if $C$ is odd (here $\frac{181-C}{2}\le C$ since $C\ge61$).

**Answer: $1\le A\le 60$, $1\le B\le 89$, $60\le C\le 178$.**

arml-1998-power-01b.title: Count $A$
arml-1998-power-01b.body:
With $B=70$: $A+C=110$ and we need $A\le70\le C$. $C=110-A\ge70$ gives $A\le40$, and $A\le 70$ then holds. So $A=1,2,\dots,40$ each gives exactly one triple ($C=109,\dots,70$). There are $40$ triples.

**Answer: 40**

arml-1998-power-02.title: Set up
arml-1998-power-02.body:
Write the angles as $k,\,2k,\,xk,\,yk,\,5k$ with $2<x<y<5$. The angle sum of a pentagon is $540^\circ$: $k(8+x+y)=540$, and $T=(x+y)k$. Put $s=x+y$; then $T=\dfrac{540s}{8+s}$, which is increasing in $s$.

Constraints on $s$: from $2<x<y<5$ we get $4<s<10$. Convexity requires every angle $<180^\circ$; the largest is $5k$, so $k<36$, i.e. $\frac{540}{8+s}<36\Rightarrow s>7$. Thus $7<s<10$.

Hence $\dfrac{540\cdot7}{15}<T<\dfrac{540\cdot10}{18}$, i.e. $252<T<300$.

Both ends are approached but not reached ($s=7$ would make the angle at $E$ equal to $180^\circ$; $s=10$ would need $x=y=5$), and since $s$ ranges over the whole interval $(7,10)$ (e.g. $x=y\approx s/2$ slightly perturbed), $T$ takes every value in between.

**Answer: $252<T<300$**

arml-1998-power-03b.title: Bound $b$
arml-1998-power-03b.body:
From $a<3b$: $200=a+b+c<4b+c$. From $b>4c$: $c<\frac b4$, so $200<4b+\frac b4$, giving $b>\frac{800}{17}\approx47.06$, i.e. $b\ge48$. For $b=48$: $c\le11$ and $a=200-48-c<144$ requires $c\ge 9$; $(a,b,c)=(141,48,11)$ works.

**Answer: 48**

arml-1998-power-03c.title: Count
arml-1998-power-03c.body:
With $c=11$: $a+b=189$, $b\ge45$ (from $b>44$) and $a<3b$ means $189-b<3b$, so $b>47.25$, $b\ge48$. Also $a\ge1$ gives $b\le188$. So $b=48,\dots,188$, which is $141$ values. The condition $b>44$ is then automatic.

**Answer: 141**

arml-1998-power-04.title: Pin down $c$
arml-1998-power-04.body:
From $5a>3b$ and $2b>c$: $a>\frac{3b}{5}>\frac{3c}{10}$ and $b>\frac c2$. Then $85=a+b+c>\frac{3c}{10}+\frac c2+c=\frac{9c}{5}$, so $c<\frac{425}{9}=47.2\ldots$.

From $c>3a$ and $5a>3b$: $a<\frac c3$ and $b<\frac{5a}{3}<\frac{5c}{9}$. Then $85<\frac c3+\frac{5c}9+c=\frac{17c}{9}$, so $c>45$.

Hence $c\in\{46,47\}$.

**$c=46$:** $a+b=39$. $c>3a$ gives $a\le15$; $2b>46$ gives $b\ge24$, so $a\le15$. $5a>3b=3(39-a)$ gives $8a>117$, $a\ge15$. So $a=15$, $b=24$, which satisfies all conditions ($46>45$, $48>46$, $75>72$).

**$c=47$:** $a+b=38$. $c>3a$: $a\le15$; $2b>47$: $b\ge24$, so $a\le14$; $5a>3(38-a)$: $8a>114$, $a\ge15$. Contradiction.

So the only solution is $(15,24,46)$. ∎

arml-1998-power-05.title: Parametrise
arml-1998-power-05.body:
Cut the square into widths $x,1-x$ and heights $y,1-y$. Reflecting the square, we may assume $x\le\frac12$, $y\le\frac12$, and swapping axes, $x\le y$. The four areas are then $xy\le x(1-y)\le y(1-x)\le(1-x)(1-y)$ (check: $x(1-y)\le y(1-x)\iff x\le y$), so $a_1=xy$, $a_2=x(1-y)$, $a_3=y(1-x)$, $a_4=(1-x)(1-y)$ with $0<x\le y\le\frac12$.

**$a_1$:** $a_1$ is the smallest of four numbers adding to $1$, so $a_1\le\frac14$, with equality for $x=y=\frac12$; and $a_1=xy>0$ can be arbitrarily small. Range $(0,\frac14]$.

**$a_2$:** $a_2=x(1-y)\le x(1-x)\le\frac14$, with equality at $x=y=\frac12$; it tends to $0$ as $x\to0$. Range $(0,\frac14]$.

**$a_3$:** $a_3=y(1-x)<y\le\frac12$; taking $y=\frac12$ and $x\to0$ gives values arbitrarily close to $\frac12$, and $x,y\to0$ gives values near $0$. Range $(0,\frac12)$.

**$a_4$:** $a_4=(1-x)(1-y)\ge\frac14$ (equality at $x=y=\frac12$) and $<1$, approaching $1$ as $x,y\to0$. Range $[\frac14,1)$.

In each case, continuity of the areas in $(x,y)$ fills in all values between the extremes found. ∎

arml-1998-power-06.title: Setup
arml-1998-power-06.body:
Cut the edges into $x,1-x$; $y,1-y$; $z,1-z$ with $x,y,z\in(0,1)$. The eight volumes are the products of one factor from each pair, e.g. $xyz$, $x y(1-z)$, $\dots$, $(1-x)(1-y)(1-z)$. They sum to $1$.

**Upper bound for $v_4$.** Pair each box with the box diagonally opposite it (swap $x\leftrightarrow1-x$, $y\leftrightarrow1-y$, $z\leftrightarrow1-z$). The product of the two volumes in a pair is $x(1-x)\,y(1-y)\,z(1-z)\le\left(\frac14\right)^3=\frac1{64}$, so the smaller one in each pair is at most $\frac18$. This gives four different boxes of volume $\le\frac18$, hence $v_4\le\frac18$. Equality holds when $x=y=z=\frac12$ (all volumes $\frac18$).

**Lower bound for $v_4$.** $v_4>0$, and it is as close to $0$ as we like: if $x\to0$, then the four boxes on the thin side all have volume $\le x$, so $v_4\le x\to0$.

**Range of $v_4$:** $(0,\frac18]$ (all values by continuity).

**$v_5$.** The four volumes $v_5,\dots,v_8$ add up to less than $1$ and are each $\ge v_5$, so $4v_5\le v_5+v_6+v_7+v_8<1$, i.e. $v_5<\frac14$. Taking $y=z=\frac12$ and $x\to0$, the four big boxes have volume $\frac{1-x}4$ each, so $v_5\to\frac14$. Also $v_5>0$, and $v_5\to0$ when $x,y,z\to0$ (then seven of the eight volumes tend to $0$).

**Range of $v_5$:** $(0,\frac14)$, neither endpoint attained. ∎

arml-1998-power-07.title: Reformulate as a game with matches
arml-1998-power-07.body:
Think of a pile of $n$ matches; the players alternately remove $a_1,a_2,\dots$ matches, each move removing at least $1$ and at most the previous move, the first move at most $n-1$. The game ends when the pile is empty. Allie moves on odd turns, so she wins iff the last match is removed by her, i.e. **the player who takes the last match wins.**

For $q\ge1$ let $p(q)$ be the largest power of $2$ dividing $q$.

**Lemma.** If $q\ge1$ matches remain and the player to move may remove any number from $1$ to $m$ with $m\ge p(q)$, then that player can force a win by removing exactly $p(q)$ matches.

*Proof (induction on $q$).* Write $q=2^e s$, $s$ odd, so $p(q)=2^e$. Remove $2^e$. If $s=1$ the pile is empty and the mover has won. Otherwise $q'=2^e(s-1)$ remain, a multiple of $2^{e+1}$, and the opponent may remove $t$ with $1\le t\le 2^e$. Since $t\le2^e<q'$, the pile is not emptied. If $t=2^w t'$ with $t'$ odd, then $w\le e<e+1$ so $q'-t$ is divisible by $2^w$ exactly, i.e. $p(q'-t)=2^w\le t$. So the first player is again allowed to remove $p(q'-t)$ matches from a smaller pile, and by the induction hypothesis wins. ∎

**If $n$ is not a power of $2$:** $p(n)<n$, so Allie may remove $p(n)\le n-1$ at her first move and wins by the Lemma.

**If $n=2^k$:** Allie removes some $a_1<n$, leaving $q=n-a_1$. Since $a_1<2^k$, $p(q)=p(a_1)\le a_1$. So Bob is allowed to remove $p(q)$ matches and wins by the Lemma.

Hence Bob has a winning strategy exactly when $n$ is a power of $2$. ∎

arml-1998-power-08.title: Zeckendorf strategy
arml-1998-power-08.body:
Use $F_1=F_2=1$, $F_3=2,\dots$ and write each $q\ge1$ uniquely as $q=F_{c_1}+\dots+F_{c_j}$ with $c_1>\dots>c_j\ge2$ and $c_i-c_{i+1}\ge2$ (Zeckendorf). Let $f(q)=F_{c_j}$ be the smallest term. The game: a pile of $q$ matches, the mover may remove between $1$ and $m$ matches (with $m$ determined by the opponent's previous move, $m=2\cdot$ previous), and whoever removes the last match wins.

**Claim.** The mover at a pile $q\ge1$ with bound $m$ wins if $m\ge f(q)$ and loses if $m<f(q)$.

*Proof by induction on $q$.* Let $s=f(q)=F_a$ with $a=c_j$.

*Case $m\ge s$.* Remove $s$ (possible: $s\le q$). If $q=s$ the mover has won. Otherwise $q'=q-s=F_{c_1}+\dots+F_{c_{j-1}}$ is a Zeckendorf representation and $f(q')=F_{c_{j-1}}\ge F_{a+2}=F_{a+1}+F_a>2F_a=2s$ (as $a\ge2$ gives $F_{a+1}>F_a$). The opponent's bound is at most $2s<f(q')$, so by induction the opponent loses.

*Case $m<s$.* The mover removes some $t$ with $1\le t\le m<s\le q$, leaving $q''=q-t>0$ and giving the opponent the bound $2t$. Write $u=s-t$, so $0<u<F_a$ and $q''=(q-s)+u$. Since $u<F_a$, the Zeckendorf representation of $u$ uses only $F_c$ with $c\le a-1$; combined with $F_{c_{1}},\dots,F_{c_{j-1}}$ (indices $\ge a+2$) it is the Zeckendorf representation of $q''$, so $f(q'')=f(u)$. It remains to show $f(u)\le 2t=2(F_a-u)$. Let $u=F_{d_1}+\dots+F_{d_i}$ ($d_1>\dots>d_i\ge2$, gaps $\ge2$), so $d_1\le a-1$ and $f(u)=F_{d_i}$. Then $d_l\le d_1-2(l-1)$, and with $m_0=d_1-2(i-1)\ge d_i\ge2$,

$u+\tfrac12F_{d_i}\le\sum_{l=0}^{i-1}F_{d_1-2l}+\tfrac12F_{m_0}\le\sum_{l=0}^{i-1}F_{d_1-2l}+F_{m_0-1}=F_{d_1+1}\le F_a,$

where the middle step uses $F_{m_0}\le2F_{m_0-1}$ and the equality comes from repeatedly applying $F_{x}=F_{x-1}+F_{x-2}$ (i.e. $F_{d_1+1}=F_{d_1}+F_{d_1-1}=F_{d_1}+F_{d_1-2}+F_{d_1-3}=\cdots$). Hence $F_a-u\ge\frac12f(u)$, so $2t\ge f(u)=f(q'')$ and by induction the opponent (with bound $2t$) wins.

**Conclusion.** Allie moves first on a pile $n$ with bound $n-1$ (she may not take everything). She wins iff $n-1\ge f(n)$. If $n$ is a Fibonacci number, $f(n)=n>n-1$ and Allie loses, so Bob wins. If not, $n$ has at least two Zeckendorf terms, $f(n)<n$, and Allie wins by removing $f(n)$. Hence Bob wins iff $n$ is a Fibonacci number. ∎
